notes: Works and treats dynamic names conservatively, but it puts the reverse-proxy-specific placeholder list and a MatchesResponse method into the generic caddyhttp CEL matcher, a layering smell; tests are strong, including a check that request-only expressions still gate transport-error retries.

Behavior is correct and well tested (including transport-error gating), but it hardcodes reverse_proxy-specific placeholder names into the generic caddyhttp CEL matcher via MatchesResponse(), a layering smell.

Production code matches the reference exactly; its request-only integration cases (escaped literal in a true comparison, status_codes == null) would fail under the old code, and it adds a ph() variant of the status-code retry test.

Code matches the reference exactly: placeholders are extracted from the checked AST, dynamic names become an empty string, and the reverse-proxy side filters on an exact response list plus a header prefix; tests cover Placeholders() and both shorthand and ph() forms.

Same sound approach as C1 and also updates the RetryMatch docs, though it drops the is_transport_error mention; several request-only integration cases (escaped literal, status_codes) evaluate to false even under the old code, so they don't separate old from new behavior.

Correct, with a clear separate dynamic flag and response-placeholder logic kept in reverseproxy; Placeholders() returns the internal slice uncloned and the RetryMatchRaw docs were edited, but the tests are very thorough (status_text, latency, ph(), escaped, prefix-lookalike).

Walks the checked CEL AST to collect literal ph() names plus a dynamic flag, and keeps the response-placeholder list in reverseproxy; its table tests directly check the escaped, status_codes, upstream.host and dynamic cases, plus an integration test that confirms the body arrives intact.

Uses CEL's MatchDescendants/FunctionMatcher idiomatically with an explicit dynamic flag; the classification logic stays in reverseproxy, and the tests cover both the classifier and the end-to-end no-retry/body-intact behavior.

Clean ReferencesPlaceholder(predicate) API keeps proxy knowledge in reverseproxy and treats dynamic names as matches; a thorough matcher-set table (comprehension, headers, escaped, status_codes) plus a body-intact integration test, with no unit test at the CEL level.

Clean ReferencesPlaceholder(predicate) API keeps the response knowledge in reverseproxy and handles dynamic names conservatively; table tests cover all the specified cases, though there is no direct celmatcher unit test.

Works, but the code is convoluted: `NewObject` and `New` re-query and compare remotes, the `objectFromFileInfo` signature changes, and zip `Open` gets odd symlink-only offset hacks. There is no collision handling, and the squashfs tests depend on an external `mksquashfs` binary.

Works, but squashfs NewObject/New rely on a convoluted double lookup with remote-mismatch checks, zip Open gains an unnecessary symlink seek special case, and the squashfs test is skipped without mksquashfs.

Core behaviour is right and well tested. Weaknesses: it ignores `Readlink` errors, `newObjectNative` calls `Info()` on every directory entry, and it adds an unrequested root-without-suffix feature. Name collisions between a real `.rclonelink` file and a symlink are not handled.

Clean, close to the reference (zip reads the target from the member, squashfs List/NewObject agree, root works with or without the suffix); minor issues are calling Info() on every entry in newObjectNative and swallowing Readlink errors.

Close to the reference: zip appends the suffix and reads the member as-is. Squashfs reads the link target and handles open ranges, and both backends keep a real `.rclonelink` member winning over a symlink. Tests are thorough and cover the hostile copy; the only oddity is the minor `isDir && !isSymlink` tweak.
Close to the reference with a simple precomputed collision map so regular .rclonelink members win, consistent squashfs lookup, root-at-symlink support, and good tests including a hostile copy.

Clean implementation for both backends. It reads link targets with a size bound and serves range/seek correctly, and real members win over translated symlinks consistently in `List` and `NewObject`. Tests even verify that the skip notice names the flag; small nit: the symlink-mode check isn't gated on non-directories.

Solid in both backends: consistent List/NewObject, regular members win name collisions, target size is bounded, range and seek are honoured via LimitedReadCloser, and tests are thorough (including log-notice and hostile-copy checks).

Adds a new shared, case-insensitive `LinkFilter` that over-filters. It drops symlinks that have members beneath them and even drops regular `.rclonelink` files that clash, diverging from the spec (likely the failed hidden test). `NewObject` now re-processes the whole directory on every lookup.

Adds a heavy new LinkFilter that silently drops any symlink with a member inside it, and drops regular .rclonelink files on clashes; this contradicts the spec's listing rules, fails a hidden test, and adds an unneeded shared file.

Sound implementation for both backends with good collision handling. However, zip silently drops any symlink that has other members beneath it or shares a name with another entry. That hides legitimate symlinks from the listing, departs from the expected behaviour, and is the likely cause of the failed hidden test.

Core translation works in both backends, but zip's addLinks drops a hostile symlink instead of listing it, which deviates from the expected listing and fails a hidden test; the dirtree manipulation is also convoluted.

The refcount logic is correct, but the patch is the most invasive: it drops the deferred unlock in Listen, changes listen() to return a listener alongside an error, moves the abstract check into listeners.go with Windows added (altering chmod behaviour elsewhere), and its race test calls t.Fatalf from a goroutine.

The refcount/master-fd fix and owned-entry unlink are correct, and it also plugs the chmod-failure leak. That required restructuring Listen's locking and making listen return a listener alongside an error; deleteListener double-close is still not idempotent, and the race test calls t.Fatalf from goroutines.

The shared refcounted socket with a master dup fixes the leaked File() dup, and the logic for double close and for close racing a listen is sound under unixSocketsMu; however, it fails every hidden test, the abstract check ignores GOOS (so '@' paths are never unlinked on non-Linux), and its abstract-socket test is vacuous because the decoy file drops the '@'.

The core refcount/master-fd fix is clean and returns net.ErrClosed directly on double close. However, isAbstractUnixSocket lacks the GOOS check, so '@' files are never unlinked on macOS/BSD, and the abstract-socket test checks a decoy without the '@' and so cannot catch the bug.

This is a well-documented shared-socket design with a correct ownership check before unlinking and OS-gated abstract handling; it also changes listenerPool accounting for reused sockets, builds verbose custom OpErrors, and fails all hidden tests because of the internal restructure.

Correct shared-socket design with linux/android abstract detection and unlink only by the registered owner. It additionally wraps reused sockets in deleteListener and changes listenerPool counting, and it hand-builds OpErrors on double close; tests are solid but the hidden suite fails to compile against the new types.

A separate state mutex lets it safely close the listener on chmod failure, and the release/unlink logic is race-safe; scope grows a lot, though, with a new mutex, listeners.go edits, and reused sockets now counted in listenerPool, while the abstract check has no OS gating and all hidden tests fail.

Race handling is sound: a separate state mutex, refs taken before using the master fd, and unlink done under the lock. But it adds a second mutex, changes listenerPool accounting for reused sockets, edits listeners.go chmod handling, and treats '@' as abstract on every OS.

This is the cleanest of the master-fd redesigns: it closes the fd before releasing, gates the abstract check on GOOS, and survives the newest holder closing first; its tests are strong, but the internal API rewrite plus the pointer-receiver deleteListener change broaden scope and break all hidden tests.

The shared refcounted socket with a master dup fd fixes the leaked File() dup, unlinks the real path under unixSocketsMu (serialized with Listen), skips abstract sockets only on linux/android, and makes double close idempotent (wrapped ErrClosed). However, rewriting the internal types drops the mapKey/count fields, so the hidden tests do not compile.
